origin.note: Georg Lankensperger devises the steering linkage in Munich; Rudolph Ackermann patents it in Britain in 1818. An earlier idea by Erasmus Darwin (1758) is not confirmed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Lankensperger

Best guess: house bells worked by wires and cranks, the system the bell crank is named after, are first recorded in a 1727 inventory of Kiveton House. Source: https://www.poplarforest.org/servant-bells-at-poplar-forest/
Best guess: eccentrics drove steam engine slide valves by about 1800 (period: around 1800). No dated first use was found.

Best guess: Villard de Honnecourt's sawmill sketch of the 1230s seems to show a four-bar linkage (period: 13th century); the source finds no unequivocal evidence before the 16th century. Source: https://gutenberg.org/cache/epub/27106/pg27106-images.html
Christoph Scheiner invents the pantograph; he publishes it in Pantographice in 1631. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christoph_Scheiner
James Watt's parallel motion for the beam engine, described in a June 1784 letter to Boulton, is built on a parallelogram linkage. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_motion_linkage
Best guess: the earliest dated use of the name lazy tongs for the scissor linkage is from 1836; the linkage is likely older. Source: https://dictionary.com/browse/lazy-tongs

Earliest dated use found: William Thomson's first tide-predicting machine makes each tidal term with a crank and slot. Older uses are likely. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide-predicting_machine
The Hierapolis sawmill relief shows a water wheel driving saws by crank and connecting rod (period: second half of the 3rd century AD). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierapolis_sawmill
Ellipsographs are believed to go back to Proclus, about 412 to 485 AD (period: 5th century AD). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipsograph
Harry Hart publishes his first inversor, built on an antiparallelogram. No earlier dated use was found. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hart%27s_inversors

Thomas Mead patents a centrifugal regulator for windmill millstones; Watt adapts it to the steam engine in 1788. Source: https://millsarchive.org/product/thomas-meads-patent-for-a-self-regulating-governor/

Elijah Galloway patents the feathering paddle wheel (the Morgan wheel), whose floats are worked by a drag-link (double-crank) linkage. Source: https://etc.usf.edu/clipart/25900/25905/feathere_pad_25905.htm
James Watt's patent specification of 28 April 1784 describes his linkage, a double rocker. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_motion_linkage

Best guess: the earliest dated description found is Huissoon and Wang's paper on a direct-drive five-bar manipulator; the linkage is surely older. Source: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/robotica/article/abs/on-the-design-of-a-direct-drive-5barlinkage-manipulator/58B2CC7F018F823112676E2093D248AA
William Murdoch makes a model oscillating cylinder engine at Boulton and Watt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscillating_cylinder_steam_engine
Best guess: the Stephenson chain is named after the Stephenson link motion of 1842; the chain's own first use is not dated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six-bar_linkage
DE-STA-CO files the patent for the first manual toggle clamp, made for the Packard Motor Car Company. Source: https://www.destaco.com/about-us.html
Best guess: the Watt chain is named after James Watt's 1784 parallel motion linkages; the chain's own first use is not dated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_motion_linkage
Theo Jansen builds his first Strandbeest, Animaris Vulgaris. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theo_Jansen
Joe Klann develops the linkage. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klann_linkage
Developed around 1900 for the twin-cylinder Lanchester car engine (period: around 1900); Philips later uses it in Stirling engines. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhombic_drive

C. P. Turner's US patent 805,041, Heating-furnace, granted 21 November 1905: skids rise through the furnace floor, lift the piles, carry them forward a step, lower and return. Source: https://patents.google.com/patent/US805041A/en
Egide Walschaerts devises the valve gear in Belgium. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walschaerts_valve_gear
Pafnuty Chebyshev reads his first memoir on approximate straight-line linkages in St Petersburg. Source: https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/hat/people/chebyshev.html
Best guess: Richard Roberts of Manchester is credited with the linkage by 1841. Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.15694
William Freemantle's British Patent 2741 covers the linkage, long before John Scott Russell. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Russell_linkage
One of the linkages in James Watt's patent specification of 28 April 1784. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_motion_linkage
Oliver Evans draws a high-pressure grasshopper beam engine. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grasshopper_beam_engine
Karl Hoecken publishes the linkage. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoecken_linkage

Nasir al-Din al-Tusi first publishes the couple in his Persian Hall-i mushkilat-i Mu'iniyya, written after 1235 and before his Tahrir al-Majisti of 1247 (period: 1235 to 1247). Source: https://ismi.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/node/2599005
Harry Hart publishes his first inversor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hart%27s_inversors
Charles-Nicolas Peaucellier announces the exact straight-line linkage; Lipkin finds it on his own in 1871. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peaucellier%E2%80%93Lipkin_linkage

Earliest dated use found: the 1912 Peugeot racing engine has its cylinders set desaxe, offset from the crankshaft. Older uses are likely. Source: https://simanaitissays.com/2019/05/24/racing-peugeots-1912-1913-part-2/

Best guess: James Nasmyth builds an early shaping machine, often called the first practical shaper; the date of the slotted-lever drive itself is not known. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Nasmyth
Joseph Whitworth creates the quick-return motion in the mid-1800s (period: mid-19th century; one source gives 1840). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quick_return_mechanism
Best guess: the drag link (patented in a paddle wheel in 1829) drives shaper rams by the mid-1800s (period: mid-19th century). No dated first use was found.
Ctesibius's water clock, as Vitruvius reports it, uses a rack and pinion (period: 3rd century BC). Source: https://geartechnology.com/ext/resources/issues/0599x/addendum.pdf
The earliest surviving gears, from China, are kept at the Luoyang Museum (period: 4th century BC). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gear

Best guess: the Antikythera mechanism is reconstructed with a crown gear meshing at a right angle (period: 2nd century BC). Source: https://www.asme.org/about-asme/engineering-history/landmarks/271-the-antikythera-mechanism

The Antikythera mechanism carries a train of some 30 gears (period: 2nd century BC, about 150 to 100 BC). Source: https://www.asme.org/about-asme/engineering-history/landmarks/271-the-antikythera-mechanism
Best guess: Robert Hooke is credited with helical (stepped) gearing (period: second half of the 17th century). Source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/helical-gearing
Gustaf de Laval introduces double helical reduction gears for his steam turbines (period: 1890s, sources give 1892 to 1894). Source: https://www.britannica.com/print/article/332618
Earliest dated drawing found: plate 78 of Agostino Ramelli's book of machines shows an internal spur gear driven by a lantern pinion. Source: https://digital.sciencehistory.org/works/h702q6667
James Watt's patent of 25 October 1781 covers William Murdoch's sun and planet gear. Source: https://beta.nationalarchives.gov.uk/catalogue/id/dd5cf905-fc3e-43eb-8862-6768a54a85ab

Archimedes is traditionally credited with the endless screw driving a toothed wheel (period: 3rd century BC). Source: https://iris.unipa.it/retrieve/e3ad8915-d631-da0e-e053-3705fe0a2b96/A21_357%20final.pdf
Best guess: Leonardo da Vinci's gear studies in the Codex Madrid I may show skew gears (period: 1493 to 1497); not confirmed. Source: https://discoveringdavinci.com/notebooks/madrid-codices/
Lorenz Braren patents the cycloidal gearbox in Germany. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycloidal_drive

Joseph Williamson's equation clock is the earliest verified use of a differential; earlier claims (Antikythera, south-pointing chariot) are unproven. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_(mechanical_device)
C. Walton Musser files the strain wave gearing patent, US 2,906,143, granted in 1959. Source: https://patents.google.com/patent/US2906143
Ernest Wildhaber of Gleason invents hypoid gearing. Source: https://www.gleason.com/gear-technology-solutions/files/basic-html/page50.html
Best guess: Giovanni de Dondi's Astrarium, finished in 1364, is reported to use non-circular gears (period: 1348 to 1364). Source: https://www.geartechnology.com/noncircular-gears
The Antikythera mechanism is the earliest surviving device with epicyclic gearing (period: 2nd century BC). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera_mechanism
Pol Ravigneaux files his patent application in France. A 1935 filing of his is cited elsewhere but not confirmed as this gearset. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravigneaux_planetary_gearset
Felix Wankel obtains his first rotary engine patent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Wankel
Best guess: star wheels with jumpers are in use in clock calendar work by about 1700 (period: 17th to 18th century). No dated first use was found.
The Geneva stop is credited to 17th or 18th century watchmakers, who used it to stop overwinding (period: 17th to 18th century). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_drive
Vitruvius describes an odometer in which one pin on the axle moves a 400-tooth wheel on by one tooth per turn (period: about 27 to 23 BC). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odometer
Best guess: internal Geneva drives appear with early film projector pull-downs (period: around 1900). No dated first use was found.

Best guess: globoidal cam index drives follow Wildhaber's globoidal worm of 1922 (period: 1920s to 1930s). No dated first roller gear indexer was found. Source: https://gearsolutions.com/departments/tooth-tips/tooth-tips-william-crosher-7/
The Banu Musa brothers in Baghdad describe an automatic organ played by a pinned cylinder (period: 9th century). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_box

Hero of Alexandria's wind organ: pegs on the wind wheel's axle lift a lever that works the air pump (period: 1st century AD). A 3rd century BC origin is claimed but not confirmed. Source: https://famousscientists.org/astonishing-ancient-greek-automatons
Best guess: flat tappets are common in early internal combustion engine valve trains (period: around 1900). No dated first use was found.
Best guess: grooved face cams for positive drive are in use in 19th century machinery (period: 19th century). No dated first use was found.
Gustav Mees is named as the first to patent desmodromic valves; the claim lacks a citation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmodromic_valve
Locomotion No. 1 of the Stockton and Darlington Railway is the first locomotive with coupling rods. Source: https://steamindex.com/library/young.htm
John Oldham invents the coupling for paddle wheels. Source: https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/people/cp136297/oldham-john
Gaspar Schott describes the joint in Technica curiosa; Robert Hooke analyses it later. Source: https://www.wikipedia.org/wiki/U-joint
Robert Hooke proposes two joints 90 degrees out of phase on an intermediate shaft to cancel the speed variation. Source: https://www.wikipedia.org/wiki/U-joint
Alfred H. Rzeppa invents his constant-velocity joint, later US patent 1,665,280. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_H._Rzeppa
Richard Schmidt files the German patent for the coupling. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schmidt_coupling
The screw press, a screw turning in a nut, was probably invented in Greece (period: 1st or 2nd century BC). Source: https://britannica.com/technology/screw
H. M. Stevenson and D. Glenn are granted patents for ball-bearing screws. Source: https://www.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_screw
William Hunter's essay on a new method of applying the screw is read to the Royal Society. Source: https://makingscience.royalsociety.org/items/l-and-p_7_179
Yang Xiong's dictionary Fangyan gives the first written reference to a belt drive, on a quilling machine. Source: https://www.wikipedia.com/wiki/V-belt
Archimedes is credited with compound pulleys, said to move a ship single-handed (period: 3rd century BC). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulley
Philo of Byzantium describes the chain drive of the polybolos repeating catapult (period: 3rd century BC). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polybolos
Milton Reeves builds a variable-speed pulley drive to control sawmill saws. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Reeves

Best guess: C. W. Hunt's patent for a variable-speed friction drive is the earliest found; friction gearing is likely older. Source: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19830011852/downloads/19830011852.pdf
James Thomson describes his disc, globe and cylinder integrator to the Royal Society. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Thomson_(engineer)
The Wadham College clock, probably by Joseph Knibb, is the oldest known anchor escapement clock. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchor_escapement

Dunstable Priory records a clock in 1283, probably a verge and foliot; the first clear drawing of a verge is Dondi's of 1364. Source: https://www.dunstablehistory.co.uk/Articles/Dunstable%20Priory%20in%201283_oldest%20recorded%20mechanical%20clock.htm
Thomas Mudge makes the first detached lever escapement, in a table clock. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Mudge_(horologist)

The Greek gastraphetes holds its drawn slider with ratchets and pawls; Zopyrus of Tarentum designs versions between 421 and 401 BC (period: late 5th century BC). Source: https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Gastraphetes

Best guess: Formgrind, later Formsprag, develops sprag overrunning clutches for an aircraft supercharger; earlier one-way clutch patents may exist. Source: https://manufacturing-today.com/news/formsprag-clutch/
Pierre Frederic Sarrus publishes the linkage in the Comptes rendus of the Paris Academy of Sciences. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarrus_linkage
Agostino Ramelli's book of machines shows swashplate pumps. Source: https://ecp.ep.liu.se/index.php/WIEFP/article/download/652/580
G. T. Bennett publishes 'A new mechanism' in Engineering. Source: https://eng.ox.ac.uk/specialstructuresgroup/research/expandable-structures-based-on-the-bennett-linkage

Earliest dated study found: Young's 1944 investigation of the cross-spring flexure pivot, cited by Haringx in 1949. Flexures were used earlier. Source: https://link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/BF02120338
Richard von Mises analyses the bistable snap-through truss in ZAMM. Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1809.04620

Best guess: the earliest dated hard source found is Reuleaux model M6, the Double Screw of Napier, made by Gustav Voigt in 1882: a cylinder with crossing helical grooves and a swivelling follower that reverses at the ends. The name points to an older origin that was not found. Source: https://dcp-production-container.library.cornell.edu/catalog/ss:372594

Warren Dyer files US 1,390,890 (granted 1921): a mower shaft with an angled middle portion, a bearing on it whose trunnions swing a head that drives the sickle. Reuleaux's spherical four-bar model C3 (1882) shows the chain itself. Source: https://patents.google.com/patent/US1390890A/en

Best guess: the earliest dated description found is No. 118 of Henry T. Brown's 507 Mechanical Movements (first published 1868): a pinion on the connecting rod meshes a fixed rack and a sliding rack above it, which moves twice as far. No earlier description or patent was found; the first patent found is US 3893644 (1975). Source: https://507movements.com/mm_118.html

Best guess: the earliest dated source found is German patent DE 271663, protected from 30 May 1911, a coupling for shafts at an angle whose bent pins slide in bored heads; it calls that arrangement already known, so the joint is older. Who Hobson was was not found. Source: https://patents.google.com/patent/DE271663C/en
